42:49: The surah closes by tracing every worldly gift back to its source: “To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and earth.” Allah governs His dominion with wisdom and creates whatever He wills. The ayah then gives an example of something people greatly desire: children. It does not say that a believer is given a particular kind of child while a disbeliever is deprived. Rather, it says: “He grants females to whom He wills”. Worldly gifts follow principles different from gifts of faith: a believer or a disbeliever may receive abundance, and either may experience restriction. The Arabic word يَهَبُ, meaning ‘bestows,’ reminds us that the gift begins with generosity and grace, not a right that a servant can impose on their Lord. Wealth or children therefore cannot be treated as a direct measure of Allah’s love.
42:50: The ayah completes the account of how these gifts are apportioned: Allah may give both sons and daughters, or He may make whomever He wills unable to have children. These differences occur throughout humanity; the commentary notes that differing circumstances of this kind occurred even in the households of prophets. Being denied a particular provision therefore does not prove that someone is dishonored, nor does receiving it prove a higher religious standing. The ayah ends: “Indeed, He is All-Knowing, Most Capable.” Withholding provision is not a lack of power, and granting it is not a coincidence. Allah can open every means; when He withholds, He does so with wisdom known to Him. A believer therefore does not surrender to despair, but gives thanks when receiving, remains patient when deprived, and trusts that this apportionment rests on knowledge and power.
42:51: After the example of worldly provision, the passage turns to the greatest religious gifts: Allah’s speech and revelation. These gifts, too, are not governed by human proposals. People cannot dictate how Allah should speak to His messenger or which signs He must give him. He chooses and selects in His wisdom. The ayah describes the ways in which He speaks: through revelation, from behind a veil—as He spoke to Moses, peace be upon him—or by sending an angelic messenger who conveys, with Allah’s permission, whatever He wills. It closes with His names: “Indeed, He is Most High, All-Wise.” He is exalted above His creation and wise in His choice and in the way He conveys His guidance.
42:52: Here is the highest provision described in the surah: “Likewise, We have revealed to you a revelation by Our command.” The Arabic word رُوحًا (rūḥan) means ‘a spirit.’ The Quran is called this because through it hearts and communities receive life: a person may be physically alive yet, without revelation, have a lifeless heart. It is then called a light, followed by the mention of guidance. This is a remarkable sequence: Allah first gives life, then the light by which the path can be seen, and then movement along it under His guidance. Before revelation, the Prophet ﷺ did not possess the details of the Book, religious laws, and worship that he would convey to people. Allah then gave him this light, and he began directing people to the straight path through instruction. The Quran is thus the highest expression of Allah’s protective care for believers and the greatest provision in which they should rejoice. How can someone seek Allah’s care while turning away from the means by which He gives their heart life and makes His will known to them?
42:53: The path to which the Quran guides is “the path of Allah, to Whom belongs all that is in the heavens and all that is on earth.” Holding fast to revelation is therefore not entering a path without an owner or helper, but following the path of the One who owns all the heavens and the earth. A believer should not fear the consequences of remaining steadfast upon the Quran as though people controlled their ultimate fate. The surah repeatedly affirms that there is no protector, refuge, or helper apart from Allah, and it concludes by declaring that all matters return to Him. The same meaning is recalled in His words: “Indeed, the One Who has ordained for you the Qur’an will bring you back home[36].” [Al-Qasas 28:85]. Holding fast to the Quran may come at a cost, but the One who made it binding is the One who controls the final outcome.
